reading.body:
Ohio's tracked 2025 to 2026 bills form the most extensive state AI legislative record in this batch, spanning a Right to Compute Act, two resolutions urging Congress to reject any federal moratorium on state AI regulation, a bill declaring AI systems nonsentient and barring them from legal personhood, and clustered bills on AI in therapy services, AI use by health insurers, and penalties for AI models that suggest self harm or harm to others.

The Ohio Right to Compute Act stands out because it frames AI policy explicitly around compute access rather than around outputs or harms, a framing that connects directly to the infrastructure question underlying most AI capability: who has the legal right to acquire and use computing resources, separate from what those resources are used to produce.

Two separate resolutions, filed roughly a year apart in December 2025 and February 2026, both urging Congress to reject a moratorium on state AI regulation, show sustained legislative concern in Ohio about federal preemption of state authority to regulate AI, repeated rather than a one time position.

The data does not indicate which of these 30 bills passed, failed, or remain pending, nor does it include bill text beyond title and number, so Ohio's actual enacted AI framework, including whether AI systems were formally denied legal personhood, is not established by this record.
